lines.note: Maguirauaxij describes something confused or difficult to distinguish, matched by perturbada and reuolta. The scan includes the t omitted from the draft’s perurbada; the headword also confirms the preceding page’s Magui- catchword.

runs.text: Mistura, ou embaraço com outra cou

lines.note: Maguire denotes mixture or confusion with something else. The final cou continues as couſa without a printed hyphen; the local Mistura spelling is retained without reclassifying its st ligature.
Sa completes couſa. Maguiremo nai cotogia asserts that the matter admits no confusion or doubt; the damaged vowel after M is a, not OCR i. The translation begins He cou-.
The assertion is translated as something clear and without doubt. This completes the nominal Maguire example before the independently inflected verb below.
The verb Maguire means becoming mixed or being exchanged/confused. Its uru and eta principal forms are retained rather than modernized to later inflections.

runs.text: de maneira que ſe não diſcirna hũa couſa da ou

lines.note: The mixture prevents one thing from being distinguished from another. The historical diſcirna remains as printed, and the final ou begins outra without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: tra. ¶ Item, Eſtar embaraçado, ou occu-

lines.note: Tra completes outra. A second sense is being entangled or occupied; the scan has two c types in occu-, correcting the draft’s single c.
Pado completes occupado. Qiôua maguiruru xiſai atte introduces having circumstances that keep the speaker occupied today; the consequence follows as ſanjenanda on the next row.
Sanjenanda completes the example: the speaker did not come because of being occupied today. The historical negative-past form and Portuguese oje are retained without modernization.
Yoni maguirete niguru describes escaping under cover of night. The Portuguese encu- continues into encuberto, keeping the printed terminal hyphen.
Berto completes encuberto com a noite. The next example concerns concealing oneself among people and divides xinobi after xi-.

runs.text: Eſtar eſcondido de mistura cõ ou-

lines.note: Nobi iru completes the concealment example, translated as remaining hidden in a mixture with other people. Ou- begins outros, not a separate alternative clause.
Tros homẽs completes the preceding translation. Sancanga maguirete aua- introduces accounts becoming confused and failing to agree; the negative ending continues below.
Nu completes auanu, not agreeing. The Portuguese explains that the accounts are entangled or confused and carries the negative clause forward.
Se acertão completes the negative statement: the accounts do not tally. The short line belongs to the accounting example, not the next compound entry.
Maguire iru, alternatively izzuru, means being among or going out amid others without being recognized. The doubled zz is visible and is not reduced to a single consonant; the gloss continues below.

runs.text: miſtura com os outros ſem ſer conhecido.

lines.note: Completes the compound’s gloss: mingling with the others without being recognized. The phrase ſem ſer conhecido specifies unnoticed participation or departure.

Maguiri is sailing on a bowline or close to the wind, as expressed by pella bulina. Enlargement shows a weak second t with surviving head and foot in itta, correcting the draft’s ita without altering the other principal forms.

runs.text: Vela que vai atraueſada, como a

lines.note: Maguiribo names a sail set transversely. The comparison starts with como a and identifies a particular type of sail on the following row.
Ceuadeira completes the sail comparison. The historical spelling is retained; the entry’s main point is its transverse setting, rather than a reconstructed rigging specification.
Magocoro is paraphrased as Macotono cocoro, a true or sincere heart. The scan uses i, with a comma, not the draft’s point; the Japanese paraphrase is not a term embedded in Portuguese.
The heart is described as sincere and true. Magocorona begins an adjectival example completed by fito below, with no hyphen supplied at this word boundary.
Fito completes Magocorona fito, a sincere and upright person. A second example begins Ma-, dividing the same adjective before its application to a horse.
Gocorona vma completes the horse example. The Portuguese calls the horse gentle and of good qualities or habits, continued by manhas below.
Manhas completes the horse’s good qualities or habits. It is the end of the Magocoro example, not an independent entry.
Magun is paraphrased as Tenguno icuſa, warfare associated with tengu. The Portuguese gloss combines war and the devil’s army; exer- begins exercito.
Cito completes exercito do Diabo. Magunuo yaburu illustrates defeating that army; the translation begins Deſ without a visible line-end hyphen, so none is supplied.
Truir completes Deſtruir: destroying the infernal army. The religious characterization is that of the dictionary’s translation.
Magure is fainting or being overcome, glossed by Eſmorecer and an attack of dizziness. The scan has an m, not the OCR sequence in, and va- continues into vagado.
Gado completes vagado. Qiga magureta illustrates being overcome or faint; the Portuguese begins saying that a dizzy spell came upon the person.
Vagado completes the example’s translation. A further sense is suffocation or choking, with the causes given on the next row; no modern clinical interpretation is imposed.
Smoke and flame illustrate the suffocation sense. Fonouoni magu- starts an example about being overcome by flame, with the verb divided before rete.
Rete completes magurete, followed by tachimachi xininu: being overcome by flame, the person died immediately. The Portuguese begins the same explanation with Afogado com.

Alabareda logo morreo completes the flame example, retaining the printed joined article and noun. At the far right, the separate opening-parenthesis marker and vagado. are overflow from the following Magure iri gloss, not part of the death example. They are restored in their physical position rather than moved down or lost.

Magure iri is equated with Tayeiru, fainting or swooning. Eſmorecer, ou dar is completed by vagado. displaced at the right of the preceding physical row; there is no missing ordinary line to insert here.
Maguſa is grass or fodder for horses. The Portuguese definition is complete on this row.

runs.text: Grades de ferrocõ q̃ gradão as Tas.

lines.note: Maguua is an iron harrow used on the Tas, rice fields. Tas is a pluralized Japanese field-name embedded in the Portuguese explanation and retains the observed italic setting; the tightly joined ferrocõ and its nasal abbreviation are not expanded.

runs.text: Certo pentem de tirar a caſpa da ca-

lines.note: Maguxi names a comb used to remove dandruff from the head. The Portuguese divides cabeça after ca-, with a visible terminal mark.

runs.text: beça, ou de pentear a cabeça.

lines.note: Beça completes cabeça, followed by the alternative function of combing the head. This closes the first Maguxi entry, before the separate horse-comb entry below.
The second Maguxi is alternatively Vmaguxi and names a comb used on horses. The action and the mane being combed are supplied in the continuation.

runs.text: penteão, & deſembaração a coma dos caualos.

lines.note: Completes the horse-comb entry: it combs and disentangles the horses’ mane. Coma is the printed mane-word here, not a comma mark or a mental-state term.
Magicai means near at hand or close before the eyes. Its gi spelling is preserved as the source’s romanization, without replacing it with modern transliteration.
Magicaſa is referred back to the same proximity sense, while Magicǒ is expressly labelled an adverb. These are printed together on one physical line; no additional line division is invented.
Mai denotes old narratives compared with romances, here verse narratives for performance rather than modern novels. The following row specifies singing and dancing.
The narratives are to be sung and danced. This closes the nominal performance-text definition before the inflected verb Mai below.
The verb Mai means dancing or singing the Mais. Mais is the pluralized Japanese performance-name inside the Portuguese definition, with its italic setting retained; the principal forms carry carons.
Mega mǒ is a figurative application concerning the eyes: the light or vision goes from them. The note records the printed expression without assigning a medical diagnosis.

Mai is a dance. Maiuo mǒ illustrates performing it, translated as singing the Mais or dancing. Chosen Cantar has a severely under-inked t, with a remaining head between n and a; the final word is visibly os, not OCR ou.
Mais completes the object of Cantar, followed by the alternative bailar. Mais is the Japanese performance-name embedded in the Portuguese sentence and retains italic type.

Mai agari describes birds rising while flying. The initial is M rather than OCR B; the spurious final l after voando was generated from the right rule, and there is no terminal hyphen to retain there.

runs.text: em voltas, como bailando: diz ſe particular-

lines.note: The birds rise in circles as though dancing. Diz ſe has i, not OCR e, and the adverb particularmente divides at the clearly printed short terminal hyphen rather than a sentence-ending point.
Mente completes particularmente. Falcons and birds called minhotos are the examples; the spelling and tilde placement in falcoẽs are preserved without imposing a modern species taxonomy.
Maiban, paraphrased as Banguegotoni, means every evening. The Portuguese tardes is retained in its historical usage.
Maibito is a person who dances, a dancer. The verb in the gloss reads baila, with the narrow dotted i, not the draft’s balla.

Maichô is paraphrased as Aſagotoni, every morning. Enlargement places the tilde over the first of the two a types in menhãas; that supplied spelling is retained rather than regularized to the more usual pattern discussed in the reference notes.
Maicocu means every hour or each time-unit, here translated Cada hora. The printed spelling retains cocu rather than expanding the Japanese expression.

runs.text: Homem que baila ao ſom dalgum inſ-

lines.note: This Maido is a person who dances to an instrument, not the every-time expression entered separately below. Inſ- begins the Portuguese name of the instrument.
Trumento completes instrumento, qualified as musical. The line closes the dancer definition before the homographic entry.
The second Maido is equated with Tabigotoni, every time. It is a separate entry from the preceding performer noun despite the identical visible headword.
Maifen, paraphrased as Fitoyegotoni, also means every time. Final S. is the upright usage label for written language; it is not part of the italic translation.
Maiguat is paraphrased as Tçuqigotoni, every month. The final bare t is preserved as the dictionary’s checked-ending notation, not expanded to a modern syllable.
Cada mes repeats the monthly sense in another Portuguese formulation. The unaccented mes is left as printed.

Maigue is followed by the preferred form Mayugue, introduced by Latin Potiùs. The gloss begins eyebrows, divided Sobran-/celhas. The second pass confirms the sloping, unserifed l as italic, unlike the upright serifed alternative-label l at c1-l016; the grave and the remainder of the italic apparatus are retained.
Celhas completes Sobrancelhas, eyebrows. It is the continuation of the Maigue/Mayugue entry, not a new headword.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de verruma, de que

lines.note: Maiguiri is a type of boring or drilling tool. The weak e between n and i belongs to maneira; the draft’s man ira is not a pair of printed words.

runs.text: vſão os torneiros com que furão contas, ou de

lines.note: Turners use the tool to drill beads. The occupation is torneiros, with a narrow i, not OCR tornetros; the gloss continues by adding other users.

runs.text: que vſão outros officiaes, como caldeireiros.

lines.note: Other craftspeople also use it, with cauldron-makers as the example. The damaged internal letters of outros are read in their surviving word shape, not as an omitted phrase.
This Maiji is paraphrased by Cotogotoni, each thing or matter. The scan reads i after a, correcting OCR Mauji; the following Maiji has a distinct time-based sense.
The second Maiji is paraphrased as Toqigotoni, every time or hour, here rendered Cada hora. Identical spelling does not collapse the two separate printed entries.
Maijit is equated with Figotoni, every day. The final t is retained as a checked ending rather than expanded to a later full syllable.
Maimai describes recurrence or frequency, glossed as something frequent or repeated. Its illustrative expression begins on the next physical row.

The example begins a formal expression of thanks for repeated kindness or service: Maimaino modifies gofǒxi. The visible caron on catajiqenǒ is retained. The mark on zǒzu- has only one strongly surviving arm; the aligned caron is retained as a usable but not graphically secure reading, with the verb continued on the next row.

The initial ru completes the preceding Japanese verb. The Portuguese says “I thank you very much for the frequent ...”; Agradeçouos is printed as one unit, and the final a- begins the noun completed below.

Completes a-/gaſalhados and the translation: frequent kind receptions or attentions, and affection. The historical gaſalhados sequence, including d, is visible and is not replaced by a more familiar modern noun.

runs.text: O que canta, ou entoa hũas hiſtorias

lines.note: This Maimai is a performer who sings or intones narratives, rather than the preceding expression meaning “each time.” The description continues onto the next row.

runs.text: como romances a q̃ chamão Mai em Iapão.

lines.note: The narratives are compared with romances and called Mai in Japan. Mai is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is visibly italic here; the Portuguese comparative wording is preserved rather than identifying a narrower modern performance genre.

Mainai is glossed as peitas, bribes or inducements. The intervening italic Varro is retained from the aligned draft: the first of its two r-like small types has no secure separate dot, although Japanese Vairo would be a plausible lexical identification. This damaged letter sequence is not silently regularized. Mainaiuo ſu- begins the example continued below.

runs.text: Dar peitas, como pera algum negocio,

lines.note: Completes ſu-/ru, “to give bribes,” and starts the explanation that these might concern a transaction or other business. The printed pera is retained; the alternatives continue on the next row.
Completes the preceding example with “or a lawsuit, etc.” Demanda belongs to the bribe-giving explanation, not to a separate Japanese entry.
Mainen is paraphrased as Toxigotoni, each year. The Portuguese Cada anno preserves the doubled n of the historical spelling.
Mainichi, paraphrased as Figotoni, means each day. The gloss is tightly set as Cadadia in the scan; the aligned joined spelling is retained rather than adding a modern word space.

Maippai is followed by the preferred form Ima ippai, introduced by Meliùs. The definition requests another serving, specified as wine below. The scan reads outra with t; the draft’s final l was the right rule, and no terminal hyphen is printed.
Completes the preceding gloss: another serving or round of wine, and the like. It does not introduce a new entry or imply a new Japanese word after ippai.

Maippaxi is assigned the preferred form Ima ippaxi, again meaning one more time. Enlargement shows a separate grave over u in Meliùs, restoring the accent omitted in the draft; ou- continues as outra below.
Tra vez completes the gloss “one more time.” Maippaxi mǒxite miǒzu illustrates saying it once more to see what happens; the two carons remain as printed.

runs.text: Dizendo outra vez verei ſe pode ſer.

lines.note: The example is translated as saying it again and seeing whether it can be done. The future verei belongs to the speaker’s trial or attempt, not an assertion that the outcome is certain.

runs.text: Mais outra vez, l, mais outra

lines.note: Ma ippen means another time, or another coat or application, the latter explained below. The internal headword spacing is retained. The right-edge enlargement shows no comma after final outra, so the draft’s terminal comma is removed.

Mão como de tinta explains the second sense as another coat, for example of paint. The separate far-right opening parenthesis and enterrar. complete the next Maiqiacu definition; they are not the letters lenterrar attached to the paint gloss. Their actual physical row is retained with named placement spans.

runs.text: S. Meter de baixo da terra, ou

lines.note: Maiqiacu is labelled S. for written usage and defined as putting beneath the earth, or burying. The final enterrar. is printed at the right of the preceding row and is retained there, not invented as a separate continuation row. The label remains in the observed italic run.

Mairaxe is giving while honoring the recipient. The principal forms ſuru and eta remain unchanged. In the Portuguese, the first letter of honrando is the italic h, not OCR b; the recipient phrase continues below.
Completes the definition: the person to whom the gift is given receives the honor. Aquem is kept joined and daa retains its double vowel; neither is silently modernized.
The noun Mairi is coming or going. It is a separate nominal entry before the two inflected verb entries, not a heading that governs their physical lineation.
This Mairi is eating or drinking said of an honored person. The gloss contains hõrada, with italic h and a nasal abbreviation, not OCR bõrada; the text is not expanded to honrada.

The final Mairi entry means going or coming. The gloss reads vir, whose italic v was misread as c in the draft. The isolated Mairiai, below it is page furniture, not a continuation of this complete definition.
